questions.passage: The following text is adapted from William Wordsworth’s 1798 poem “Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey.” Once again Do I [u][vocab]behold[/vocab][/u] these steep and lofty cliffs, Which on a wild secluded scene impress Thoughts of more deep seclusion; and connect The landscape with the quiet of the sky.
questions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “behold” most nearly mean?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Possess

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regard

choices.label: C
choices.text: Omit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Escape

explanation.short: Here, “behold” means to look at the cliffs—that is, to regard them.
explanation.key_evidence: “Once again / Do I behold these steep and lofty cliffs”
explanation.why_correct: The text places “behold” directly before a visible landscape and says the speaker does it “once again,” so the verb describes seeing or regarding the cliffs.
explanation.detailed: The speaker is returning to a familiar view and looking at the cliffs, the secluded scene, and the sky. In this setting, “regard” preserves the visual action of “behold,” whereas the other verbs introduce ownership, exclusion, or flight.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Possess”) is incorrect because it would mean owning the cliffs, but the poem describes the speaker viewing them.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Regard”) is correct because it means look at or observe, matching the speaker’s renewed sight of the cliffs.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Omit”) is incorrect because it means leave something out; the speaker instead attends closely to the landscape.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Escape”) is incorrect because it means get away, which conflicts with the speaker’s return to and contemplation of the scene.

questions.passage: Although oil shocks—such as the 10% rise in oil prices in November 1970—can strongly affect individual consumers, Gbadebo Oladosu and colleagues have shown that at the level of national economies, their effects are often quite [vocab]______[/vocab]. The effect of recent oil shocks on the gross domestic product of Germany, for example, was only slightly greater than zero.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: variable

choices.label: B
choices.text: persistent

choices.label: C
choices.text: subdued

choices.label: D
choices.text: beneficial

explanation.short: The near-zero GDP effect shows that national-level effects can be subdued, or limited.
explanation.key_evidence: Germany’s GDP effect was “only slightly greater than zero.”
explanation.why_correct: The text contrasts strong effects on individual consumers with a German national effect barely above zero, so the blank must characterize national effects as muted rather than strong.
explanation.detailed: “Subdued” precisely expresses reduced intensity. The example supplies a concrete measure—an effect only slightly above zero—that supports this meaning and does not establish variability, duration, or benefit.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“variable”) is incorrect because it concerns differences or fluctuation, but the example establishes small magnitude, not variation among effects.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“persistent”) is incorrect because it concerns how long an effect lasts; the passage gives its size, not its duration.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“subdued”) is correct because it means restrained or muted, fitting an effect that is only slightly greater than zero.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“beneficial”) is incorrect because it would assign a positive value to the shocks, whereas the text merely says their GDP effect is small.

questions.passage: Writer Lydia Davis observed that while [vocab]______[/vocab] literary forms, such as the poem, are recognizable as such even as they evolve, there are pathbreaking “intergeneric” forms that might, for example, use elements of both fables and realist narratives to create something unclassifiable. Davis’s own very short literary pieces arguably fit in this category, since they straddle the line between prose and poetry.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: innovative

choices.label: B
choices.text: elusive

choices.label: C
choices.text: established

choices.label: D
choices.text: ambiguous

explanation.short: Recognizable conventional forms are established, unlike the pathbreaking intergeneric forms.
explanation.key_evidence: Poems remain recognizable; the contrasting forms are “pathbreaking” and “unclassifiable.”
explanation.why_correct: The text sets familiar forms such as poems against new forms that cross genre boundaries, so the blank needs a word meaning already recognized and conventional: “established.”
explanation.detailed: The while-clause creates a contrast between categories readers can identify even as they evolve and creations that resist classification. Calling the first group “established” makes that contrast coherent.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“innovative”) is incorrect because it would make both sides novel, weakening the contrast with “pathbreaking” forms.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“elusive”) is incorrect because it suggests the forms are difficult to identify, contradicting the statement that they are recognizable.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“established”) is correct because it names forms with recognized conventions, such as the poem, and supplies the intended contrast.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“ambiguous”) is incorrect because it implies unclear classification, a quality assigned to the intergeneric forms instead.

questions.passage: Mauricio Drelichman and Hans-Joachim Voth’s analysis of the debt repayments and expenditure of the government of Philip II (who ruled an empire including Spain and Milan from 1556 to 1598) found a seeming contradiction: although the government had several short-term cash shortages, it ran an even larger surplus than did the government of eighteenth-century Britain, a nation considered [vocab]______[/vocab] of fiscal virtue.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a sanction

choices.label: B
choices.text: a paradox

choices.label: C
choices.text: an exemplar

choices.label: D
choices.text: an omen

explanation.short: Britain serves as an exemplar—a model—of fiscal virtue.
explanation.key_evidence: Britain is the benchmark whose surplus makes Philip II’s larger surplus surprising.
explanation.why_correct: The text treats eighteenth-century Britain as a standard of excellent public finance, so “an exemplar of fiscal virtue” correctly identifies it as a model against which Philip II is compared.
explanation.detailed: The seeming contradiction depends on Britain’s respected fiscal reputation: exceeding its surplus is noteworthy. “Exemplar” supplies exactly that sense of a representative model.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“a sanction”) is incorrect because it is a penalty or authorization, not a nation admired as a financial model.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“a paradox”) is incorrect because it would call Britain itself contradictory, but the contradiction concerns Philip II’s shortages and surplus.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“an exemplar”) is correct because it means an outstanding model, matching Britain’s role as the standard of fiscal virtue.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“an omen”) is incorrect because it is a sign of a future event; the passage discusses Britain’s reputation, not a prediction.

questions.passage: The following text is from Anthony Trollope’s 1855 novel [i]The Warden[/i]. Charles James is the son of a high-ranking clergy member. Charles James was an exact and careful boy; he never committed himself; he well knew how much was expected from the eldest son of the Archdeacon of Barchester, and was therefore mindful not to mix too freely with other boys. He had not the great talents of his younger brothers, but he exceeded them in judgment and propriety of demeanour; his fault, [u]if he had one[/u], was an over-attention to words instead of things; there was a thought too much finesse about him, and, as even his father sometimes told him, he was too fond of a compromise.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the function of the phrase “if he had one” in the text as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acknowledges that the qualities in Charles James the narrator goes on to describe may not actually be undesirable characteristics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It concedes that Charles James’s attempts to be held in respect are sometimes fruitless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It signals a shift in focus from describing Charles James’s good qualities to criticizing his tendency to place too much value on artfulness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It anticipates readers’ objections to the narrator’s criticism of Charles James’s faults.

explanation.short: “If he had one” hesitates to label Charles James’s finesse and caution as a genuine fault.
explanation.key_evidence: The narrator writes “his fault, if he had one,” before naming overattention to words and compromise.
explanation.why_correct: The supplied text and evidence establish the connection: By inserting a conditional qualification immediately after “his fault,” the narrator leaves open whether the traits that follow are truly undesirable; the phrase softens rather than launches the criticism.
explanation.detailed: The surrounding description praises Charles James’s judgment and propriety, then tentatively identifies possible shortcomings. The phrase makes the negative label provisional, which is exactly the acknowledgment described in A.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“It acknowledges that the qualities in Charles James the narrator goes on to describe may not actually be undesirable characteristics.”) is correct because it accurately captures the hedge: the narrator allows that the forthcoming qualities may not deserve to be called faults.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“It concedes that Charles James’s attempts to be held in respect are sometimes fruitless.”) is incorrect because it invents failed attempts to win respect; the passage says he behaves carefully but never reports such attempts failing.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“It signals a shift in focus from describing Charles James’s good qualities to criticizing his tendency to place too much value on artfulness.”) is incorrect because it assigns the shift to the phrase itself, although “his fault” and the following description create the shift; “if he had one” qualifies it.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“It anticipates readers’ objections to the narrator’s criticism of Charles James’s faults.”) is incorrect because it claims the narrator anticipates reader objections, but no readers or objections are mentioned; the uncertainty is the narrator’s own.

questions.passage: The establishment of urban green spaces for the abatement of fine particulate matter and other major air-pollutant concentrations is gaining public support, but urban planners must proceed with caution given subtleties in the body of evidence for the strategy’s efficacy. High-level reports have attributed pollutant reductions to cities’ inclusion of green spaces; however, one study found that while trees are negatively associated with air pollutants when considered on a citywide scale, at the street level, this association is minimal and at times positive. Because research tends to focus on large-scale effects in cities, decision-makers may be unaware that those outcomes are not always generalizable across spatial scales.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It outlines a problem that is of growing public concern, explains why an innovative solution to that problem is challenging to implement, and then suggests the importance of researching alternative solutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It addresses an appealing approach to a prevalent problem, illustrates that the approach is not as uniformly successful as it may seem, and then further emphasizes the importance of recognizing nuances in the research on that approach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It details an initiative implemented in response to certain research findings, identifies an apparent inconsistency within those findings, and then explains how that inconsistency has typically been accounted for.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It establishes the growing intensity of a public concern, details the most common method of mitigating that concern, and then refers to evidence that the method is broadly ineffective.

explanation.short: The passage introduces green spaces, qualifies their apparent success across scales, and urges attention to that nuance.
explanation.key_evidence: Trees correlate negatively with pollution citywide, but the street-level association is minimal or sometimes positive.
explanation.why_correct: The text first presents a popular anti-pollution strategy, then uses scale-dependent findings to show that its results are not uniform, and finally warns decision-makers against generalizing citywide research.
explanation.detailed: Each paragraph move appears in B: appeal, qualification, and a caution about research nuance. The study does not prove green spaces broadly ineffective; it shows that an effect observed at one spatial scale may not transfer to another.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“It outlines a problem that is of growing public concern, explains why an innovative solution to that problem is challenging to implement, and then suggests the importance of researching alternative solutions.”) is incorrect because it wrongly says the text calls for alternative solutions; it calls for caution in interpreting research on green spaces.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“It addresses an appealing approach to a prevalent problem, illustrates that the approach is not as uniformly successful as it may seem, and then further emphasizes the importance of recognizing nuances in the research on that approach.”) is correct because it tracks all three moves, including the appealing strategy, uneven scale-specific results, and final warning about generalizability.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“It details an initiative implemented in response to certain research findings, identifies an apparent inconsistency within those findings, and then explains how that inconsistency has typically been accounted for.”) is incorrect because it says an inconsistency has typically been accounted for, but the ending says decision-makers may be unaware of it.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“It establishes the growing intensity of a public concern, details the most common method of mitigating that concern, and then refers to evidence that the method is broadly ineffective.”) is incorrect because it overstates the evidence as broad ineffectiveness, although the citywide association is favorable and only street-level results are mixed.

校订说明：编辑校订：删去了将“首部小说”笼统等同于“作者出版的第一本书”的多余定义；原有题干、选项和考点不变。

[i]The Skin I’m In[/i] was Sharon G. Flake’s debut novel. It was published in 1998. Debut novels are especially interesting to literary critics (people whose job it is to evaluate books) and readers because these books offer a look at new voices in the literary world.
questions.prompt: According to the text, what is someone who professionally evaluates books called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bookseller

choices.label: B
choices.text: An author

choices.label: C
choices.text: A literary critic

choices.label: D
choices.text: A book publisher

explanation.short: A literary critic professionally evaluates books.
explanation.key_evidence: The parenthetical defines literary critics as people whose job is to evaluate books.
explanation.why_correct: The question asks for an occupational title, and C matches the definition stated in the passage. No inference about Flake's career or the novel's publication date is necessary.
explanation.detailed: Locate the words that restate the question: professionally evaluates books means evaluates books as a job. Those words appear immediately after literary critics in parentheses, identifying the profession. Selling, writing and publishing books are different activities, so the other three titles do not answer the stated question.

choice_analysis.A: A bookseller sells books; the passage asks for the person whose job is evaluating them.
choice_analysis.B: An author writes books. Flake is the author discussed, but the requested occupation is the evaluator's.
choice_analysis.C: A literary critic is explicitly defined in the parenthetical as someone who evaluates books professionally.
choice_analysis.D: A book publisher prepares and issues books for publication, not the occupation named by the passage's evaluation definition.

questions.passage: The following text is adapted from L.M. Montgomery’s 1923 novel [i]Emily of New Moon[/i]. Emily, a young girl who lives on a farm run by her aunt Elizabeth, wants to be a published writer someday. One of the things they [argued] about was the fact that Emily, as Aunt Elizabeth discovered one day, was in the habit of using more of her egg money to buy paper than Aunt Elizabeth approved of. What did Emily do with so much paper? They had a fuss over this and eventually Aunt Elizabeth discovered that Emily was writing stories. Emily had been writing stories all winter under Aunt Elizabeth’s very nose and Aunt Elizabeth had never suspected it. She had fondly supposed that Emily was writing school compositions.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Emily forgot to buy eggs when she was supposed to.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aunt Elizabeth thinks Emily should spend more time at school.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aunt Elizabeth is surprised to find out that Emily has been writing stories.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emily is relieved to learn that Aunt Elizabeth enjoys reading Emily’s stories.

explanation.short: Aunt Elizabeth unexpectedly discovers that Emily has secretly been writing stories all winter.
explanation.key_evidence: Elizabeth “had never suspected” the stories and thought the pages were school compositions.
explanation.why_correct: The text centers on Elizabeth questioning Emily’s paper purchases and then being surprised to learn that the pages contain stories, not the schoolwork she had assumed.
explanation.detailed: The conflict over egg money leads to the passage’s key discovery: Emily has pursued creative writing unnoticed. C summarizes both the discovery and Elizabeth’s surprise without adding later reactions that the text never gives.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Emily forgot to buy eggs when she was supposed to.”) is incorrect because it misreads “egg money”: Emily spends some of it on paper; the passage never says she forgot to buy eggs.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Aunt Elizabeth thinks Emily should spend more time at school.”) is incorrect because it invents a complaint about time at school, whereas Elizabeth objects to how much money Emily spends on paper.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Aunt Elizabeth is surprised to find out that Emily has been writing stories.”) is correct because it captures Elizabeth’s surprise upon discovering that Emily’s supposed compositions are actually stories.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Emily is relieved to learn that Aunt Elizabeth enjoys reading Emily’s stories.”) is incorrect because it adds relief and Elizabeth’s enjoyment of the stories, neither of which appears in the excerpt.

questions.passage: A student in an economics course is examining the decline since 1950 in average hours worked per person per year in various nations due to both increased productivity and the adoption of policies that limit working hours. The first task in this investigation is to determine how the decline in Finland compares to that in other countries. The student finds that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the student’s conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the percent decrease in hours worked was greater in Finland than it was in Denmark, Canada, or Peru.

choices.label: B
choices.text: though the decline in number of hours worked in Finland was less than that in Denmark and Canada, it was greater than that in Peru.

choices.label: C
choices.text: while the number of hours worked rose in Finland between 1950 and 2017, it declined in Denmark, Canada, and Peru.

choices.label: D
choices.text: though the decline in number of hours worked in Finland was greater than that in Denmark and Peru, it was less than that in Canada.

explanation.short: Finland’s 394-hour decline falls between Peru’s smaller decline and the larger Canadian and Danish declines.
explanation.key_evidence: Declines: Peru 225 hours; Finland 394; Canada 513; Denmark 649.
explanation.why_correct: The supplied text and evidence establish the connection: The table shows 394 fewer hours in Finland, which is less than the 513-hour Canadian and 649-hour Danish drops but greater than Peru’s 225-hour drop, exactly the ordering in B.
explanation.detailed: Compute each absolute change from the table’s change column and compare magnitudes. Finland is neither the largest nor the smallest decline: it ranks above Peru and below Canada and Denmark.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“the percent decrease in hours worked was greater in Finland than it was in Denmark, Canada, or Peru.”) is incorrect because it incorrectly uses percent change: Finland’s 19% decrease is smaller than Canada’s 23% and Denmark’s 32%, though larger than Peru’s 10%.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“though the decline in number of hours worked in Finland was less than that in Denmark and Canada, it was greater than that in Peru.”) is correct because it states the correct absolute comparison: 394 is below 513 and 649 but above 225.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“while the number of hours worked rose in Finland between 1950 and 2017, it declined in Denmark, Canada, and Peru.”) is incorrect because it reverses Finland’s direction; its hours fall from 2,053 in 1950 to 1,659 in 2017.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“though the decline in number of hours worked in Finland was greater than that in Denmark and Peru, it was less than that in Canada.”) is incorrect because it incorrectly puts Finland’s 394-hour decline above Denmark’s 649-hour decline.

questions.passage: Ratified in 2017 by two-thirds of World Trade Organization member nations, the Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) is a trade-reform measure that aims to reduce redundant customs procedures and other costly aspects of international trade. In a 2021 report, economist Jayson Beckman modeled global market prices of several agricultural commodities under both the TFA and an alternative trade-reform scenario: removal of agricultural tariffs (taxes on imports that generally increase prices on imported goods). After reviewing data from the report, a student concludes that overall, consumers of the commodities listed in the table would likely benefit more from the TFA than they would from tariff removal.
questions.prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student’s claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Under the tariff-removal scenario, the average prices of processed foods, wheat, and fruits and vegetables would decrease by more than 1%, while the average price of rice would decrease by less than 1%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under the tariff-removal scenario, the average price of processed foods would increase, but the average prices of wheat and rice would decrease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Under the TFA scenario, the average prices of all four commodities would decrease, whereas under the tariff-removal scenario, only the average price of processed foods would decrease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Under the TFA scenario, the average price of rice would decrease by a smaller amount than any of the other three commodities’ prices would, whereas its average price would increase under the tariff-removal scenario.

explanation.short: Every listed price decreases under the TFA, while only processed foods decrease under tariff removal.
explanation.key_evidence: TFA changes are all negative; tariff removal is negative only for processed foods (−1.00%).
explanation.why_correct: The table indicates broader consumer price reductions under the TFA: all four commodity changes are below zero, whereas tariff removal raises three prices and lowers only processed foods.
explanation.detailed: Because consumers generally benefit from lower prices, the sign pattern directly supports the student’s comparison. C uses every commodity and contrasts the two scenarios rather than isolating one product.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Under the tariff-removal scenario, the average prices of processed foods, wheat, and fruits and vegetables would decrease by more than 1%, while the average price of rice would decrease by less than 1%.”) is incorrect because it contradicts the tariff-removal column: fruits and vegetables, wheat, and rice increase rather than decrease.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Under the tariff-removal scenario, the average price of processed foods would increase, but the average prices of wheat and rice would decrease.”) is incorrect because it reverses all three cited directions; processed foods fall, while wheat and rice rise under tariff removal.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Under the TFA scenario, the average prices of all four commodities would decrease, whereas under the tariff-removal scenario, only the average price of processed foods would decrease.”) is correct because it accurately contrasts four TFA decreases with the single tariff-removal decrease for processed foods.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Under the TFA scenario, the average price of rice would decrease by a smaller amount than any of the other three commodities’ prices would, whereas its average price would increase under the tariff-removal scenario.”) is incorrect because it accurately describes rice alone, but one commodity cannot support the student’s overall claim as effectively as the full four-item comparison.

questions.passage: Issuing a one-dollar coin yields positive seigniorage—the profit generated when the face value of a coin exceeds the unit cost of producing it—for Singapore’s government, which in turn can be used to fund such services as transportation. Some countries, such as the Netherlands, have ceased manufacturing certain coins because their production created negative seigniorage. In an economics class discussing the data in the table, one student argues that in 2023, the one-cent coin was the least financially sensible for the US to produce, while another student argues that the five-cent coin was.
questions.prompt: Based on the information in the text and the table, the two students most likely disagree about the answer to which question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When evaluating the financial implications of issuing a coin, which is more important, the total seigniorage from issuing that coin or the seigniorage per dollar when issuing that coin?

choices.label: B
choices.text: If issuing a given coin results in negative seigniorage per dollar issued, can that be changed to positive seigniorage per dollar issued by reducing the cost of issuing the coin?

choices.label: C
choices.text: If issuing a given coin results in positive seigniorage per dollar but not as much positive seigniorage per dollar as issuing a different coin does, does it make financial sense to continue issuing the first coin?

choices.label: D
choices.text: When determining whether it makes financial sense to issue a given coin, which is more important, the total value of the units of that coin produced or the gross cost of issuing that coin?

explanation.short: The students rank the coins differently because total loss and loss per dollar point to different coins.
explanation.key_evidence: Nickel total seigniorage: −$92.6 million; penny seigniorage per dollar: −$2.08.
explanation.why_correct: The supplied text and evidence establish the connection: The table makes the five-cent coin worst by total seigniorage but the one-cent coin worst by seigniorage per dollar, so the disagreement turns on which of those two measures matters more.
explanation.detailed: One student can cite the penny’s larger loss per dollar, while the other can cite the nickel’s larger aggregate loss. A names exactly this competing standard for financial sensibility.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“When evaluating the financial implications of issuing a coin, which is more important, the total seigniorage from issuing that coin or the seigniorage per dollar when issuing that coin?”) is correct because it identifies the two measures that produce the competing judgments: total seigniorage and seigniorage per dollar.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“If issuing a given coin results in negative seigniorage per dollar issued, can that be changed to positive seigniorage per dollar issued by reducing the cost of issuing the coin?”) is incorrect because it asks how cost changes might improve a coin’s return, but neither student’s ranking depends on a hypothetical cost reduction.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“If issuing a given coin results in positive seigniorage per dollar but not as much positive seigniorage per dollar as issuing a different coin does, does it make financial sense to continue issuing the first coin?”) is incorrect because it concerns two coins with positive per-dollar seigniorage, while both the penny and nickel have negative figures.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“When determining whether it makes financial sense to issue a given coin, which is more important, the total value of the units of that coin produced or the gross cost of issuing that coin?”) is incorrect because it separates total value from gross cost, but the stated disagreement is resolved by the table’s derived seigniorage measures, not either input alone.

questions.passage: Describing adverbs as “silly,” novelist Chuck Palahniuk is one of several authors and literary critics who have recommended minimizing the use of adverbs, especially those ending in [i]-ly[/i] (e.g., “graciously”), in works of fiction. To investigate the prevalence of [i]-ly[/i] adverbs in novels, author and statistician Ben Blatt used natural language processing—machine learning technology that reads and interprets text—to calculate the rates at which these words occur in the novels of William Faulkner, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1949. Blatt concluded that in Faulkner’s oeuvre, there is a negative correlation between [i]-ly[/i] adverb proliferation and perceived literary merit.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly illustrate the pattern Blatt identified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whereas Faulkner’s acclaimed novel [i]The Sound and the Fury[/i] has one of the lowest [i]-ly[/i] adverb rates among Faulkner’s works, F. Scott Fitzgerald’s classic novel [i]The Great Gatsby[/i] has the lowest [i]-ly[/i] adverb rate among Fitzgerald’s novels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In [i]The Sound and the Fury[/i], which is widely recognized as a literary masterpiece, Faulkner used 42 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words, whereas in his less-acclaimed novel [i]Soldiers’ Pay[/i], Faulkner used 148 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In his celebrated novel [i]Light in August[/i], Faulkner used 67 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words, whereas 67% of celebrated authors’ novels that have fewer than 50 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words have been classified as great by critics.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whereas Faulkner used on average 92 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words in the 19 novels of Faulkner’s that Blatt investigated, Toni Morrison, winner of the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature, used on average 76 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words in her novels.

explanation.short: A highly acclaimed Faulkner novel has far fewer -ly adverbs than a less-acclaimed Faulkner novel.
explanation.key_evidence: [i]The Sound and the Fury[/i]: 42 per 10,000 words; [i]Soldiers’ Pay[/i]: 148.
explanation.why_correct: The text defines a negative within-Faulkner correlation: as perceived literary merit rises, -ly adverb frequency should fall. B supplies both sides of that relationship within his novels.
explanation.detailed: The acclaimed masterpiece’s rate is less than one-third of the less-acclaimed novel’s rate, directly illustrating the claimed inverse pattern. Comparisons with other authors do not test the conclusion about Faulkner’s oeuvre.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Whereas Faulkner’s acclaimed novel [i]The Sound and the Fury[/i] has one of the lowest [i]-ly[/i] adverb rates among Faulkner’s works, F. Scott Fitzgerald’s classic novel [i]The Great Gatsby[/i] has the lowest [i]-ly[/i] adverb rate among Fitzgerald’s novels.”) is incorrect because it compares Faulkner with Fitzgerald and does not connect differing adverb rates to differing merit among Faulkner’s own novels.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“In [i]The Sound and the Fury[/i], which is widely recognized as a literary masterpiece, Faulkner used 42 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words, whereas in his less-acclaimed novel [i]Soldiers’ Pay[/i], Faulkner used 148 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words.”) is correct because it pairs greater merit with 42 -ly adverbs and lesser merit with 148, directly displaying the negative correlation.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“In his celebrated novel [i]Light in August[/i], Faulkner used 67 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words, whereas 67% of celebrated authors’ novels that have fewer than 50 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words have been classified as great by critics.”) is incorrect because it gives only one Faulkner work and an unrelated percentage about other celebrated authors, so it cannot establish the within-oeuvre pattern.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Whereas Faulkner used on average 92 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words in the 19 novels of Faulkner’s that Blatt investigated, Toni Morrison, winner of the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature, used on average 76 [i]-ly[/i] adverbs per 10,000 words in her novels.”) is incorrect because it compares Faulkner’s average with Toni Morrison’s average; it says nothing about variation in merit among Faulkner’s books.

questions.passage: Students in a biology class investigated why individual house mice ([i]Mus musculus[/i]) can differ from one another in their circulating sodium level. The students compared wild-type mice and knockout mice, which are mice with specific genes deactivated, when mice of each type were placed in similar naturalistic environments and taken for periodic blood sampling. Finding that knockout mice with the gene [i]Asb5[/i] deactivated tended to have lower concentrations of sodium in their blood than did wild-type mice, the students concluded that differences in circulating sodium level among house mice in nature are solely attributable to variations in the level of expression of [i]Asb5[/i].
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the students’ conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some wild-type mice were very similar to the knockout mice with regard to circulating sodium level but showed a wide variety of levels of expression of [i]Asb5[/i].

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sampling of house mice captured in natural settings shows that individual mice can differ from one another in the level of expression of [i]Asb5[/i].

choices.label: C
choices.text: The level of expression of [i]Asb5[/i] does not appear to affect the functioning of any other genes in house mice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mice with [i]Asb5[/i] deactivated were identical to the wild-type mice except with regard to circulating sodium level.

explanation.short: A makes the proposed exclusive link between Asb5 expression and sodium less convincing.
explanation.key_evidence: Wild-type mice with widely varying Asb5 expression nevertheless have sodium levels similar to the knockout mice.
explanation.why_correct: This weakens the generalization that variation in this gene's expression alone accounts for sodium differences; the other options either fit that idea or strengthen the comparison.
explanation.detailed: The knockout comparison suggests Asb5 can matter, but it does not by itself establish that expression variation is the only influence in nature. A's mismatch between widely varied expression and similar sodium makes that exclusive interpretation less secure. It does not prove a one-to-one relationship is biologically required or that Asb5 has no effect; weakening is less demanding than deductively disproving the conclusion.

choice_analysis.A: Correct: similar sodium despite diverse expression undermines the simple exclusive explanation.
choice_analysis.B: Natural expression variation is compatible with the students' proposed cause.
choice_analysis.C: No effect on other genes does not establish another cause of sodium variation.
choice_analysis.D: Otherwise identical groups differing in sodium would strengthen the knockout comparison.

questions.passage: Neuroscientist Artin Arshamian and his team sought to determine what affects a person’s perception of an odor as pleasant: is it culture, personal taste, or aspects of human anatomy? The team assessed odor preferences in ten groups of people with different modes of living (urban, agricultural, and hunter-gatherer) including urban dwellers from a large city in Thailand and Chachi people from a small community in Ecuador. The team observed that across cultures, people generally rated odors about the same: vanillin, which smells like vanilla, was typically rated more pleasant than isovaleric acid, which smells like human sweat. The team therefore concluded that ______
questions.prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: a person who lives in an urban area is more likely to encounter the odor of vanillin than is a person who lives in a small community.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a person’s mode of living likely doesn’t have a large influence on that person’s perception of whether an odor is pleasant or unpleasant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: a person who perceives certain odors as pleasant will likely perceive the odors as roughly equal in pleasantness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: culture likely plays more of a role in a person’s perception of how pleasant an odor is than does human anatomy.

explanation.short: Similar odor rankings across very different groups indicate that mode of living has little influence on pleasantness judgments.
explanation.key_evidence: Ten urban, agricultural, and hunter-gatherer groups generally ranked vanillin above isovaleric acid.
explanation.why_correct: The text reports broadly shared odor preferences despite contrasting modes of living, so the results support the conclusion that mode of living is not a major determinant of perceived pleasantness.
explanation.detailed: The study varies culture and lifestyle yet observes the same general ordering of odors. That consistency supports B, while it cannot establish how often people encounter vanillin or isolate anatomy as the dominant cause.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“a person who lives in an urban area is more likely to encounter the odor of vanillin than is a person who lives in a small community.”) is incorrect because it speculates about exposure frequency in urban and small communities, a variable the study does not report.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“a person’s mode of living likely doesn’t have a large influence on that person’s perception of whether an odor is pleasant or unpleasant.”) is correct because it draws the warranted inference from similar ratings across urban, agricultural, and hunter-gatherer groups.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“a person who perceives certain odors as pleasant will likely perceive the odors as roughly equal in pleasantness.”) is incorrect because it says pleasant odors will be rated roughly equal to one another, but the example explicitly ranks vanillin above isovaleric acid.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“culture likely plays more of a role in a person’s perception of how pleasant an odor is than does human anatomy.”) is incorrect because it claims culture matters more than anatomy, contrary to the cross-cultural similarity and without anatomical comparison data.

questions.passage: The towns Entebbe and Jamame are both located almost directly on the ______ they are in different countries. Entebbe is in Uganda, while Jamame is in Somalia.

explanation.short: A comma plus “but” correctly joins two independent clauses that contrast shared latitude with different countries.
explanation.key_evidence: Clause 1: both towns lie near the equator; clause 2: they are in different countries.
explanation.why_correct: The text contains two complete sentences on either side of the blank, and their ideas contrast, so Standard English requires the coordinating conjunction “but” preceded by a comma.
explanation.detailed: “The towns ... are located ... on the equator” and “they are in different countries” each have a subject and finite verb. Choice B forms a valid compound sentence and signals the intended contrast.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“equator”) is incorrect because it leaves two independent clauses adjacent with no punctuation or conjunction, creating a run-on.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“equator, but”) is correct because it supplies comma + coordinating conjunction “but,” the correct boundary and logical link.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“equator,”) is incorrect because it uses only a comma between independent clauses, producing a comma splice.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“equator that”) is incorrect because it makes “that they are in different countries” modify “equator,” an illogical and ungrammatical attachment.

questions.passage: Having trained as astronauts for years, ______

choices.text: August 2, 1991, was when space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i] took flight with five crew members aboard.

choices.label: B
choices.text: it was August 2, 1991, when five crew members took flight aboard space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i].

choices.label: C
choices.text: five crew members took flight aboard space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i] on August 2, 1991.

choices.label: D
choices.text: space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i] took flight on August 2, 1991, with five crew members aboard.

explanation.short: The introductory phrase must modify the five crew members, the people who trained as astronauts.
explanation.key_evidence: “Having trained as astronauts for years” logically describes the five crew members.
explanation.why_correct: Because the opening participial phrase describes people, the subject immediately after the comma must be “five crew members”; C places that logical subject in the required position.
explanation.detailed: A participial opener attaches to the following grammatical subject. Only C says that the trained crew members took flight, avoiding the absurd implication that a date, dummy “it,” or the shuttle trained as astronauts.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“August 2, 1991, was when space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i] took flight with five crew members aboard.”) is incorrect because it makes “August 2, 1991” the modifier’s target, implying that a date trained as an astronaut.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“it was August 2, 1991, when five crew members took flight aboard space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i].”) is incorrect because it places dummy “it” after the phrase, so the trained people are not the grammatical subject being modified.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“five crew members took flight aboard space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i] on August 2, 1991.”) is correct because it immediately names the five crew members who completed the astronaut training and then states their action.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“space shuttle [i]Atlantis[/i] took flight on August 2, 1991, with five crew members aboard.”) is incorrect because it makes the space shuttle the subject, incorrectly suggesting that [i]Atlantis[/i] trained as an astronaut.

explanation.short: The plural subject “lawmakers” takes “designated,” and singular possessive “state’s” modifies “official fossil.”
explanation.key_evidence: New Jersey lawmakers performed the designation; the fossil belongs to one state.
explanation.why_correct: The sentence needs a plural subject, a past-tense verb, and a singular possessive determiner. “Lawmakers designated the state’s” supplies all three forms correctly.
explanation.detailed: There is no possession after “lawmakers,” so no apostrophe belongs there. By contrast, “state’s” must show that the official fossil is New Jersey’s.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“lawmakers designated the state’s”) is correct because it correctly uses plural “lawmakers,” verb “designated,” and singular possessive “state’s.”
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“lawmakers designated the states”) is incorrect because it uses plural “states” where the possessive “state’s” is needed before “official fossil.”
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“lawmaker’s designated the states”) is incorrect because it turns “lawmaker’s” into a possessive even though the sentence needs a subject, and “states” also lacks the possessive apostrophe.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“lawmaker’s designated the state’s”) is incorrect because it has the correct “state’s” but incorrectly makes “lawmaker’s” possessive instead of using plural “lawmakers.”

questions.passage: Nicosia is home to roughly 27 percent of Cyprus’s total population. This means that about 1 in 4 ______ live in Cyprus live in Nicosia!

choices.text: people

choices.label: B
choices.text: people who

choices.label: C
choices.text: people,

choices.label: D

explanation.short: The restrictive clause “who live in Cyprus” identifies which people the statistic concerns.
explanation.key_evidence: The intended unit is “1 in 4 people who live in Cyprus.”
explanation.why_correct: The text must restrict “people” to Cyprus residents before stating that those residents live in Nicosia, so the relative pronoun “who” is necessary and no comma should separate the essential clause.
explanation.detailed: Without the relative clause, the two verbs “live ... live” have no grammatical connection. Adding unpunctuated “who” makes the first verb part of an essential modifier and leaves the second as the main predicate.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“people”) is incorrect because it produces the ungrammatical sequence “people live in Cyprus live in Nicosia” with no relative pronoun.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“people who”) is correct because it creates the grammatical restrictive noun phrase “people who live in Cyprus.”
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“people,”) is incorrect because it inserts a comma but still omits the pronoun needed to introduce the relative clause.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“people, who”) is incorrect because it treats “who live in Cyprus” as nonessential, implying all people live there; the clause is essential to define the population counted.

questions.passage: In the Persian language, people commonly begin a folktale with a phrase that roughly translates to “there was and there was not.” In English, beginning with the phrase “once upon a time” is common. choices.label: C
choices.text: they are

choices.label: D

explanation.short: The singular noun “a folktale” requires the singular pronoun-and-verb pair “it is.”
explanation.key_evidence: Antecedent: “a folktale”; completed clause: “the language in which it is being told.”
explanation.why_correct: The text refers to one folktale, so the relative clause must use singular “it” and singular auxiliary “is” before “being told.”
explanation.detailed: The phrase “in which” introduces a passive progressive clause describing the telling of the folktale. “It is being told” agrees in number and completes that verb phrase.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“they were”) is incorrect because it uses plural “they” and past “were,” neither of which agrees with singular “a folktale” or the present generalization.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“these are”) is incorrect because it uses plural demonstrative “these,” which has no plural antecedent in the sentence.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“they are”) is incorrect because it uses plural “they are,” creating a number mismatch with “a folktale.”
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“it is”) is correct because it correctly pairs singular “it” with “is” to refer back to the singular folktale.

questions.passage: [i]Thraxas[/i] by Martin Scott, [i]Richard Matheson: Collected Stories[/i] by Richard Matheson, and [i]Strange Tales[/i] by Rosalie Parker are all pieces of literature that have won the prestigious World Fantasy ______ the works received the honor in the categories of novel, collection, and anthology, respectively.

explanation.detailed: The first clause ends after “World Fantasy Award.” The next begins “the works received,” which cannot be attached by a bare comma and does not need an added coordinating conjunction after the blank.

choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Award;”) is correct because it places a semicolon between the two independent clauses, creating a valid sentence.

questions.passage: If you were to view the Namarunu volcano in Kenya from above, you might notice that its low profile and gently sloping sides make it look a bit like a shield lying flat on the ground. ______ it makes sense that Lydia Jennings and other volcanologists classify Namarunu as a shield volcano.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Therefore,

choices.label: D

questions.passage:
Text 1

In separate studies, Marine Fernandez and colleagues and Xinhua He and colleagues examined whether plants transfer nutrients to one another using a common mycorrhizal network (CMN)—a lattice of fungal strands in the soil. Fernandez and colleagues excluded all pathways other than the CMN by using barriers to keep the plants’ root systems separate while allowing mycorrhizal strands through—a crucial step He and colleagues’ study did not take.

Text 2

Fernandez and colleagues took the necessary precaution of separating the plants’ root systems (thereby excluding root-to-root transmission). However, any barrier used must allow the thread-like hyphae of a CMN to pass through, and this permeability would also allow liquids through. Thus, the researchers’ experimental design cannot ensure that any nutrient transfer observed can be attributed to a CMN and not to some other pathway.
questions.prompt: Based on the texts, which choice best describes a similarity in the points of view presented in Text 1 and Text 2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each text attempts to dispel a common misunderstanding about the likelihood of plant-to-plant nutrient transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each text assumes that most nutrient transfer between plants is via a CMN.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each text analyzes methods for studying CMN nutrient transfer in order to propose an alternative method of study.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each text critiques the methodology of a study about nutrient transfer via a CMN.

explanation.short: Each text questions whether a study’s method can isolate nutrient transfer through a CMN.
explanation.key_evidence: Text 1 faults He’s missing root barrier; Text 2 faults Fernandez’s liquid-permeable barrier.
explanation.why_correct: Text 1 criticizes He and colleagues for failing to exclude root pathways, while Text 2 criticizes Fernandez and colleagues for leaving liquid transfer uncontrolled; both are methodological critiques.
explanation.detailed: The texts target different studies and different possible confounds, but share the view that experimental design limits what can be attributed to a CMN. Neither proposes a replacement method.

choice_analysis.A: Choice A (“Each text attempts to dispel a common misunderstanding about the likelihood of plant-to-plant nutrient transfer.”) is incorrect because it invents a widespread misunderstanding about how likely nutrient transfer is; both texts instead discuss causal isolation in experiments.
choice_analysis.B: Choice B (“Each text assumes that most nutrient transfer between plants is via a CMN.”) is incorrect because it says both assume most transfer uses CMNs, whereas both question whether observed transfer can be assigned to that pathway.
choice_analysis.C: Choice C (“Each text analyzes methods for studying CMN nutrient transfer in order to propose an alternative method of study.”) is incorrect because it adds the purpose of proposing an alternative study method, but neither text offers a complete replacement design.
choice_analysis.D: Choice D (“Each text critiques the methodology of a study about nutrient transfer via a CMN.”) is correct because it captures the shared act of identifying a methodological weakness in research on CMN nutrient transfer.
